docs.title: About
docs.text:
I'm Robert N. Myhre, an independent technology researcher with a background in enterprise infrastructure and architecture.

I investigate questions about systems: what they actually do, how components interact, where constraints emerge, and what happens when assumptions meet implementation. My interests range across GPU systems and distributed AI, networking, security, automation, and governed agentic systems.

My technical background informs which questions I notice. The investigations here are ones I chose to pursue.

docs.title: Why I investigate
docs.text:
Curiosity often starts with a small discrepancy: a feature that should work but does not; a topology diagram that seems to promise a performance outcome; a platform abstraction that might reduce complexity; or an AI workflow whose authority boundary is not yet clear.

I might build a prototype, capture measurements, draw an architecture, or work through a set of constraints. I try to record what I believed at the start, which claims the evidence actually supports, and what changed my mind.

A completed implementation is not the definition of success. Discovering that an idea does not work as expected can be just as useful. Some conceptual investigations may remain unproven.

docs.title: Areas that interest me
docs.text:
• AI infrastructure, GPUs, topology, distributed inference, and observability
  • Human–AI collaboration, communication, and agency
  • Networking and distributed systems
  • Identity, security, trust boundaries, and governed automation
  • Cloud and infrastructure platforms
  • Emerging ideas that raise worthwhile technical questions

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
My professional foundation is in networking and infrastructure architecture, supported by hands-on engineering, technical writing, and teaching. That experience supplies context for the research but is not its subject.

For code and underlying research repositories, see GitHub.

docs.title: Research Methodology
docs.text: This is my record of independent investigations. Some ideas have been tested extensively; others are early architectural explorations with open questions.

docs.title: The starting point is a question
docs.text: An investigation might begin with an unexpected observation, an architectural possibility, a technology I want to understand, or an assumption worth challenging. The question may evolve as I learn. I try to preserve that evolution rather than rewrite the story as though the outcome was obvious from the beginning.

docs.title: Different investigations need different methods
docs.text:
• Experimental research uses measurement and comparison to examine actual behavior.
  • Prototype-driven research implements enough of a system to test a hypothesis or expose architectural constraints.
  • Architectural research explores models, relationships, tradeoffs, and boundary conditions through explicit reasoning.
  • Conceptual investigations develop possible systems without claiming that their designs have been implemented or validated.

These are useful descriptions, not mandatory document templates. A project can involve more than one method.

docs.title: Evidence and claims
docs.text:
I distinguish:

  • Question or hypothesis: what I want to understand or suspect may be true.
  • Proposed design: what I think might satisfy a set of constraints.
  • Observed result: what a particular experiment or implementation actually showed.
  • Validated finding: what is supported by defined tests and their limitations.
  • Open question: what the current evidence does not settle.

Prototype results do not establish production suitability. A reference architecture can be useful while remaining unproven. A stalled or rejected approach is still worth documenting when the reasoning is informative.

docs.title: Publication boundaries
docs.text: Investigations published here begin with questions I choose to explore. Research notes focus on the question, method, evidence, limitations, and what I learned.

docs.title: No required outcome
docs.text: An investigation can remain conceptual, be deferred, change direction, or end in a negative result. This site is a record of questions I chose to explore and what I was able to learn—not a list of technologies I set out to endorse.

docs.title: GPU Communication Boundaries
docs.text: Context: Independent AI infrastructure research Status: Completed intra-node investigation; cross-node work deferred Domain: GPU placement, NUMA/PCIe topology, NCCL transport selection, collective and application performance Repository: View the public case-study repository on GitHub

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This started with a limitation in my home quad-GPU server that bothered me. Two GPUs shared each NUMA node, while communication between NUMA domains crossed the SYS path through the inter-socket boundary. I initially wondered whether that topology could still be useful for multi-tenant workloads. That led to the more interesting question: how much did the extra distance actually matter, and would the workload notice?

The study used a four-V100 PCIe workstation and a rented four-L40S cloud instance. I expected the socket boundary to explain a meaningful performance difference. Controlled comparisons showed otherwise: placement alone did not explain the results. The communication mechanism selected by NCCL mattered more, and its benchmark performance did not reliably predict application throughput.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Separate three questions that a topology diagram alone cannot answer:

  • What paths does the hardware support?
  • Which transport does the runtime actually select?
  • How much does that choice affect the application?

The comparisons varied GPU placement and transport policy within each platform. The two systems provided complementary experiments, rather than a controlled V100-versus-L40S ranking.

docs.title: Architecture and Method
docs.text:
The investigation combined topology and P2P capability captures, NCCL transport logs, repeated all-reduce benchmarks, and a 124-million-parameter PyTorch DDP training workload using synthetic tokens in fp32.

Runs were interleaved across configurations, with medians, observed spreads, host state, and GPU telemetry retained. Application transport captures were checked separately because PyTorch bundled a different NCCL version.

Two discoveries on the L40S instance required revising the experiment: the default four-GPU ring used host staging, while default two-GPU jobs used P2P. Planned policy contrasts therefore had to be checked against the selected transport before their performance could be interpreted.

Explore the visual comparison: Two Platforms, One Boundary →

docs.title: Placement and mechanism required separate controls
docs.text:
Under matched transports, crossing the socket boundary produced no measurable collective penalty in the tested comparisons.

Changing the mechanism did affect bandwidth: forcing P2P improved the V100 same-socket pair by approximately 15%; disabling P2P reduced L40S pair bandwidth by approximately 18% at both placements.

docs.title: Capability did not establish runtime selection
docs.text:
NCCL selected host staging on paths where P2P was available. On the tested L40S instance, default selection also changed with communicator size.

A supported hardware path and a configured policy were insufficient evidence of the path used by a particular job.

docs.title: Faster collectives did not guarantee faster training
docs.text:
The mixed-transport rings underperformed the all-host-staged rings by approximately 10% on V100 and 37% on L40S.

Application effects were much smaller. The L40S same-NUMA pair's approximately 18% collective-bandwidth loss accompanied a training-throughput difference within the observed spread. Some collective improvements accompanied application regressions.

docs.title: Architectural Finding
docs.text:
Before paying for topology-aware placement or forcing a transport policy, verify the selected mechanism and measure whether the workload benefits.

I came into the investigation expecting topology to explain the performance difference. I left it unwilling to accept a topology diagram or collective benchmark alone as sufficient evidence for a placement recommendation. I would now want to see the transport the workload actually used and whether the measured communication advantage survived at the application level.

The transferable result is the measurement approach: distinguish hardware capability, runtime behavior, and application impact; revise comparisons when observations contradict their assumptions; and retain unresolved causes as open questions.

docs.title: Scope and Evidence
docs.text:
These findings describe one workstation, one cloud instance, and one synthetic training workload. Observed spreads are descriptive comparisons, not statistical equivalence tests. Cross-node communication, NVLink, RDMA, and network fabrics were not tested.

The accumulation experiment improved throughput, but also changed optimizer-update frequency; it did not isolate communication time.

The public repository contains the full case study, selected evidence, platform qualification methodology, two decision records, a transport-discovery field note, and five unchanged research instruments. The complete run archive and provisioning toolkit are not published.

docs.title: Intelligence Placement Under Constraint: A Framework for Distributed AI
docs.text:
Context: Independent architecture research Status: Framework retained from a retired white paper Domain: Distributed AI, intelligence placement, decision flow, governance, observability, failure modes

This framework originated in a broader white paper exploring distributed intelligence in enterprise environments. The original paper was later retired as the industry moved faster than parts of its framing, but several architectural concepts remained useful: intelligence placement, context and decision flow, silent failure, distributed control boundaries, and constraint-driven architecture.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
As AI moves into enterprise operations, the architecture problem becomes larger than deciding where to host a model.

Intelligence may execute across endpoints, local or edge infrastructure, enterprise platforms, and centralized model environments. Each location offers different advantages and constraints.

The useful architectural question is therefore not:

Where should the AI platform live?

It is:

Where should a particular form of intelligence execute, given the constraints of the environment?

Those constraints can include latency, data locality, governance, cost, resilience, operational complexity, and trust.

The framework treats centralized and distributed intelligence as complementary patterns rather than competing architectures.

docs.title: Intelligence Placement as an Architecture Decision
docs.text: A useful way to reason about distributed AI is as a set of execution layers.

docs.title: Device or endpoint
docs.text:
The closest layer to the user, sensor, or source of data.

This layer is useful when:

  • latency must be very low
  • connectivity may be unreliable
  • sensitive data should remain local
  • filtering or preprocessing can reduce what must travel upstream

docs.title: Local or gateway infrastructure
docs.text:
A site-local or regional layer with more compute and broader context than an endpoint.

This layer can:

  • aggregate signals from multiple sources
  • provide local inference or enrichment
  • reduce dependence on centralized connectivity
  • retain data closer to its source

docs.title: Enterprise core
docs.text:
The enterprise layer is likely to remain the primary execution point for many complex AI workflows.

It provides:

  • broader organizational context
  • access to enterprise systems and data
  • stronger governance and audit controls
  • more efficient shared compute
  • integration across multiple workflows and models

docs.title: Model factory
docs.text:
Training, fine-tuning, evaluation, and model lifecycle activities form another layer.

The model factory is not necessarily the center of the operational system. It supplies models and capabilities to the layers where intelligence is actually consumed.

The architecture emerges from how responsibilities are divided across these layers.

docs.title: The System Is Defined by Flow
docs.text:
Component placement alone does not describe the behavior of a distributed AI system.

The more useful model is flow.

Context flows upstream.

Signals are captured, filtered, enriched, retrieved, and combined as they move toward systems with broader awareness.

Decisions flow downstream.

Recommendations, policies, outputs, and constraints move back toward users, applications, or execution environments.

Context flows upstream toward broader awareness, while decisions flow downstream toward action.

There can also be lateral flows between models, agents, tools, or systems operating at the same layer.

This creates an architecture defined not only by connectivity, but by:

  • where context is gathered
  • where decisions are made
  • what information is permitted at each stage
  • how decisions are constrained
  • where trust boundaries exist
  • how failure propagates through the decision process

For infrastructure architects, this is a familiar way of thinking applied to a new object.

Networks have long been understood through flows, constraints, and failure domains.

Distributed AI adds decision flow to that model.

docs.title: Security Becomes a Continuous Property
docs.text:
Traditional infrastructure security often focuses on boundaries: who can connect, what can cross a zone, and which systems can communicate.

AI-driven systems introduce additional questions.

A request may influence data retrieval, model reasoning, external tools, or infrastructure actions.

Security therefore has to consider:

  • Intent — what is the request attempting to accomplish?
  • Context — what information may be accessed?
  • Action — what is the system permitted to do?
  • Outcome — how is the resulting output validated?

Controls may need to exist at multiple points in the system rather than at one centralized boundary.

That can include:

  • prompt and intent controls
  • dynamic context scoping
  • tool and action authorization
  • deterministic policy enforcement
  • output validation
  • auditing and traceability

The security architecture increasingly follows the decision flow itself.

docs.title: Silent Failure and Decision Observability
docs.text:
One of the more important differences between traditional infrastructure and AI-driven systems is that a system can be technically healthy while producing a degraded decision.

Consider a system that successfully answers a request but was unable to retrieve part of the required operational context.

Traditional monitoring may report:

  • the service is available
  • latency is normal
  • the request completed
  • no dependency reported an outage

Yet the recommendation may have been generated from incomplete information.

The system is operational, but its decision conditions are degraded.

This creates a class of silent failures that normal infrastructure monitoring does not fully expose.

A useful distinction is:

Infrastructure observability asks whether the system is functioning.

Decision observability asks under what conditions the decision was made.

Meaningful AI observability may therefore need to include:

  • context completeness
  • data lineage
  • decision traceability
  • model confidence
  • confidence in the data used by the model
  • visibility into degraded decision conditions

Availability alone is not enough.

docs.title: Constraints as Forcing Functions
docs.text:
Distributed AI architecture is not determined only by technical possibility.

Several forces shape where intelligence can realistically execute.

docs.title: Latency
docs.text: Some decisions benefit from local execution because centralized inference introduces unacceptable delay.

docs.title: Data locality and governance
docs.text: Policy, privacy, regulatory, or operational boundaries may limit where information can move.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: Centralized infrastructure can provide higher utilization and simpler operations. Distributed execution may improve locality or resilience while increasing infrastructure and management cost.

docs.title: Operational complexity
docs.text: Every additional execution environment creates lifecycle, observability, support, and coordination requirements.

docs.title: Vendor and platform dependency
docs.text: Enterprise AI systems will often combine internal systems with external models, platforms, and managed services. Those dependencies can reduce visibility or architectural control.

docs.title: Trust
docs.text:
A technically capable system may still fail operationally if the people responsible for outcomes cannot understand or trust its behavior.

These constraints do not produce one ideal architecture.

They determine which combination of centralized and distributed patterns is practical.

docs.title: Architectural Finding
docs.text:
Centralized and distributed intelligence are not opposing architecture choices.

Centralization often provides:

  • operational simplicity
  • stronger governance
  • shared infrastructure efficiency
  • easier auditing and lifecycle management

Distribution can provide:

  • lower latency
  • stronger locality
  • resilience to connectivity constraints
  • tighter control over sensitive information

Most enterprise architectures will likely combine both.

The architectural task is to determine which intelligence belongs where, under which constraints, and with which control boundaries.

docs.title: What This Framework Demonstrates
docs.text:
This work was not intended as a prediction of a particular distributed-AI product architecture.

It was an attempt to create a reusable way to reason about systems whose correctness increasingly depends on more than moving data successfully.

The durable questions are:

  • Where is intelligence placed?
  • What context is available at each layer?
  • How do context and decisions move?
  • Where are authority and control applied?
  • What failures remain invisible to normal monitoring?
  • Which constraints determine whether distribution is actually justified?

Technologies and platforms will continue to change.

Those questions remain useful because they focus on the structure and behavior of the system rather than on a particular implementation.

docs.title: MCP Platform Case Study: Build, Validate, Reject
docs.text: Context: Independent architecture research Status: Completed; platform development deliberately closed Domain: MCP infrastructure, identity, security boundaries, workload isolation, platform architecture Repository: View the public case study on GitHub

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
I built and validated a centralized Model Context Protocol (MCP) service harness to test whether multiple MCP services could share a common access, execution, and security boundary without distributing service credentials to every client or exposing the services directly.

The implementation worked.

The reusable-platform hypothesis did not.

Rather than continue extending a technically functional design, I closed the project when the evidence showed that the abstraction was not reducing the cost or complexity of adding real services.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Determine whether a centralized MCP platform could provide reusable infrastructure for:

  • per-client access identity
  • restricted MCP execution
  • isolated and immutable workloads
  • controlled network access
  • credential containment
  • lifecycle and drift management
  • multiple MCP services behind a common platform boundary

The goal was not simply to make an MCP server work remotely. The architecture needed to make the next service materially easier and safer to add.

docs.title: Architecture and Validation
docs.text:
The platform used per-client SSH identities, a forced-command dispatcher, restricted privilege escalation, and ephemeral containerized MCP workloads.

Workloads were constrained through explicit execution and network boundaries, including destination-specific egress controls, immutable image pinning, supply-chain verification, session isolation, and reconciliation logic.

A NetBox MCP server became the first real service used to test whether the platform abstraction held.

End-to-end validation demonstrated:

  • remote MCP access through the complete platform boundary
  • successful read-only NetBox operations from a remote AI client
  • concurrent session isolation
  • workload cleanup after session completion
  • restricted egress to the approved upstream service
  • recovery across Docker and host restarts
  • explicit handling of policy drift and unknown workload state

docs.title: Architectural Finding
docs.text:
NetBox exposed three weaknesses that the generic test workload had not:

  1. Service integration remained highly customized. Adding the first real MCP service still required substantial service-specific launch, lifecycle, installation, policy, credential, and validation work.

  2. Authentication did not become downstream authorization. The platform could identify the initiating client at the MCP access boundary, but that identity did not propagate into authorization at the upstream service.

  3. Marginal service cost remained too high. The platform was centralizing MCP services without abstracting enough of the work required to operate them.

The architecture therefore failed its most important test: the next real service was not becoming sufficiently easier to add.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
Development of the custom host-based platform was deliberately stopped. The working NetBox MCP deployment was retained; what ended was continued development of the custom harness surrounding it.

The decision was not based on implementation failure. It was based on evidence that continuing would mean investing further in custom versions of capabilities increasingly resembling general orchestration primitives such as reconciliation, workload isolation, lifecycle management, recovery, and policy enforcement.

Several architectural principles survived the rejected implementation:

  • per-client identity
  • verified server and workload identity
  • isolated and immutable workloads

Those principles, along with unresolved identity and authorization questions, became requirements for the next architecture rather than reasons to preserve the original implementation.

docs.title: What This Demonstrates
docs.text:
This project is an example of architecture as hypothesis testing rather than implementation completion.

The useful result was not simply that the system worked. It was determining where the design stopped providing enough architectural value to justify further investment.

The full public repository includes the decision records, validation findings, diagrams, implementation components, retrospective, and the transition into the next Kubernetes and IAM-focused investigation.

docs.title: MoE Routing Observability
docs.text: Context: Independent AI infrastructure research Status: Completed research series Domain: Multi-GPU inference, Mixture of Experts, observability, NUMA/PCIe topology, model placement Repository: View the public research repository on GitHub

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
I instrumented Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on a four-GPU NVIDIA V100 server to understand what sparse models actually demand from constrained infrastructure.

The investigation focused less on model quality than on infrastructure behavior: router decisions, expert placement, memory requirements, PCIe and NUMA traffic, runtime compatibility, and whether commonly reported performance measurements were actually telling the full story.

Several initial assumptions did not survive measurement.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Make MoE inference observable enough to answer infrastructure questions that aggregate throughput alone cannot:

  • How does expert routing affect device and interconnect behavior?
  • What does model placement cost across NUMA boundaries?
  • Does successful quantized loading prove that the expert weights were actually quantized?
  • Can runtime configuration be trusted simply because an API accepts and reports it?
  • How much of an apparent performance difference survives repeated trials and better controls?
  • What infrastructure burden remains even when only a subset of experts is active for each token?

The goal was not to optimize a benchmark score. It was to understand which measurements are required before drawing architecture conclusions from MoE workloads.

docs.title: Architecture and Method
docs.text:
The primary platform was a dual-NUMA server with four NVIDIA V100 16 GB GPUs connected through PCIe without NVLink.

Experiments used controlled model placement, router-logit capture, GPU and PCIe telemetry, per-parameter dtype inspection, repeated benchmark trials, and explicit evidence records.

The research was structured so that claims remained tied to captured evidence and corrections remained visible when later experiments invalidated an earlier conclusion.

docs.title: Placement costs can be invisible to throughput
docs.text:
Cross-NUMA expert dispatch produced substantially higher PCIe traffic than same-NUMA dispatch in the tested runs, while aggregate token throughput remained effectively unchanged.

The important result was not that one placement was universally slower. It was that a throughput-only view would have hidden a large difference in interconnect behavior.

docs.title: Successful model loading did not prove quantization succeeded
docs.text:
A MoE model requested with quantization could load successfully while large portions of the expert pool remained unquantized.

This demonstrated that configuration intent and successful startup were insufficient validation. Per-parameter inspection was required to determine what actually happened.

docs.title: Accepted configuration did not prove runtime behavior
docs.text:
A vLLM expert-placement configuration was accepted and reflected through the configuration interface, but later validation showed that the requested placement policy had not actually taken effect.

Repeated trials also disproved an apparent performance improvement that had initially looked significant.

docs.title: Better controls changed conclusions
docs.text:
NUMA pinning and repeated measurements exposed confounding factors in earlier experiments.

Rather than preserve the original findings, the research record retains the corrections and documents why the conclusions changed.

docs.title: Architectural Finding
docs.text:
MoE reduces active computation per token, but it does not eliminate the infrastructure burden of placing and operating the full model.

Sparse routing also introduces behavior that can remain invisible when infrastructure is evaluated only through aggregate application metrics.

For architecture and operations, meaningful MoE observability therefore needs to include more than tokens per second. It can require visibility into:

  • router behavior
  • model and expert placement
  • actual parameter dtypes
  • GPU memory pressure
  • NUMA locality
  • PCIe traffic
  • runtime compatibility
  • repeated-trial variance

The specific measurements in this project are constrained to the tested hardware. The instrumentation and validation approach are the more transferable result.

docs.title: What This Demonstrates
docs.text:
This research demonstrates an evidence-driven approach to AI infrastructure.

The useful findings included both expected behavior and negative results: configurations that silently failed, conclusions that reversed under better controls, performance differences that disappeared under repeated trials, and infrastructure costs that application-level metrics did not expose.

The public repository contains the methodology, findings, lab guides, instrumentation scripts, captured results, reproduction guidance, and provenance describing how AI assistance was used during the research.

docs.title: Project Boundary: Where AI reasoning ends and operational authority begins
docs.text:
Exploring how AI agents can participate in consequential infrastructure operations without inheriting uncontrolled authority over the systems they influence.

Enterprise infrastructure automation is something we've been doing for decades. We have mature tools for deploying configurations, provisioning infrastructure, applying software updates, and performing operational tasks across thousands of systems. The questions change when we introduce AI into the decisions surrounding those operations.

An AI agent can interpret information from multiple sources, identify relationships, evaluate alternatives, and recommend a course of action. Those capabilities could be valuable in enterprise operations, particularly where engineers spend considerable time investigating conditions before deciding what automation should do. But recommending an action is different from having the authority to execute it.

That difference became the foundation for Project Boundary, an independent architecture research project exploring how probabilistic AI reasoning could participate in infrastructure operations while remaining subject to deterministic controls and enterprise governance.

The project began with a hypothetical enterprise Linux patching scenario, with no customer environment or production deployment involved. The scenario was realistic enough to investigate the architectural decisions that come into play once AI can influence consequential infrastructure changes. My objective was to determine what kind of architecture would make AI participation in those operations governable.

As the investigation developed, two questions came to define almost everything that followed:

What do I trust the model to consume?

What do I trust the model's reasoning to influence?

These sound like straightforward questions. In practice, they led to some of the project's more useful architectural findings.

docs.title: Starting with the architecture
docs.text:
I chose Linux patching because it illustrates a familiar operational problem. Tools such as Ansible Automation Platform can execute patching workflows reliably, package management systems can identify available updates, and monitoring systems can provide operational telemetry. None of those capabilities resolves the surrounding decisions. Which systems should be patched together? What application dependencies exist? Could taking a particular group of servers offline affect service availability? What evidence should establish that the operation succeeded? And if something goes wrong, how does the system decide what happens next?

These questions frequently require information from multiple enterprise systems, along with operational knowledge that may not be represented in a single authoritative source. This is where AI reasoning could help. Working alongside existing automation, an agent might interpret operational context, identify dependencies, recommend maintenance groups, or investigate unexpected outcomes. Allowing an agent to perform that reasoning does not mean it should also decide what actions are authorized.

I began by developing a Reference Architecture that separated three responsibilities. AI components capable of interpreting context and developing proposals would handle reasoning. Deterministic orchestration would handle control, verifying evidence, enforcing constraints, and governing workflow progression. Authority would remain with explicitly governed human decisions or previously approved enterprise policies. The execution systems would continue performing the actual infrastructure changes.

This separation established an architectural principle that remained consistent throughout the investigation:

AI may make decisions within an authorized boundary, but it cannot independently define, expand, or waive that boundary.

The principle carries particular weight with probabilistic systems. A model can produce a technically plausible recommendation that is incomplete, incorrect, or based on misleading information. Improving the model may reduce those risks, but it doesn't eliminate the need for independent operational controls. The architecture therefore needed to treat AI output as something to evaluate rather than something that automatically carried authority.

docs.title: The other side of the problem: what enters the model?
docs.text:
Much of the early architecture focused on what an AI agent should be allowed to do. As I worked through the design, I became increasingly interested in what the agent was being allowed to know, or more precisely, what information it was allowed to use as the basis for operational reasoning.

Enterprise AI systems rarely operate on carefully curated prompts alone. They consume tickets, inventory records, runbooks, monitoring results, application descriptions, configuration details, and information retrieved through tools. Some of that information is structured and governed. Some is free-form text. Some may be outdated or contradictory, and some could contain malicious instructions intended to change the behavior of the model.

An agent could therefore reach an unsafe conclusion without ever receiving direct authority to execute an action. The architecture might correctly prevent the model from calling an execution tool, yet still permit the model to influence the inputs used by the system that makes the final decision. I began treating the information entering AI reasoning as a separate security boundary.

The initial design included a dedicated semantic screening function to evaluate potentially hostile natural-language content before admitting it into the reasoning context. Before implementing the larger architecture, I also conducted a small supporting experiment to investigate whether a dedicated screening model and a reasoning model could coexist on the same GPU. The purpose was to explore the practicality of model-based screening as an architectural component.

The results were encouraging, with some qualifications. On the tested NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada, the two models occupied 16,559 MiB of the GPU's measured 20,475 MiB total, leaving 3,916 MiB free on that basis. Co-residency was practical, but it didn't provide useful parallel inference in the tested configuration. Across a 17-case comparison, the pipelined arrangement was about 1.2% slower per case than sequential execution. That gave me a workable basis for local semantic screening without requiring a separate GPU for each model. The single-GPU guardrail research includes the measurements and their limitations.

The screening function was intentionally constrained, with bounded outputs, no operational tools, no persistent memory, and no authority to modify infrastructure. It could contribute evidence about potentially unsafe content, but it could not decide what operational consequences should follow. That limit mattered from the beginning, and implementation would make it matter more.

docs.title: Using implementation to challenge the architecture
docs.text:
After developing the Reference Architecture, I began implementing it through a series of vertical slices. I wanted enough working functionality to test whether the architectural boundaries behaved the way I expected them to, and a complete enterprise automation platform was never the intention.

That approach produced useful findings early. The implementation reinforced the need for AI models to produce proposals and evidence rather than executable commands. It also demonstrated why safety decisions could not depend solely on affirmative judgments from an AI model. Human authorization needed to bind to a specific operation, ambiguous execution outcomes needed to be reconciled before another mutation, and validation needed to establish more than whether an automation job returned a successful status. Each of these findings influenced the implementation.

Eventually I encountered a different problem. The first implementation had accumulated a series of local changes. Each change addressed a legitimate issue, but the combined result was becoming increasingly difficult to reason about. I could have continued fixing it, but I was no longer confident that doing so was the best way to evaluate the architecture, so I restarted.

I preserved the code, tests, findings, and failed assumptions from the first implementation as research evidence. The second implementation began with a thinner end-to-end path, carrying forward the architectural principles that had survived the first investigation.

This became one of the project's clearer methodological lessons. An implementation can fail to express an architecture without necessarily proving the architecture itself is wrong. Conversely, successfully executing a workflow does not establish that the intended architectural controls are actually present. The responsibility is to tell those conditions apart and revise the appropriate part of the system. For Boundary, implementation was a research instrument, and preserving the architecture's testability mattered more than preserving every line of code.

docs.title: When a deterministic control doesn't have enough evidence
docs.text:
One of the project's main findings involved evidence acquisition. The architecture already required deterministic verification before an operation could proceed. The reasoning agents could propose actions, but a separate control component would determine whether the necessary conditions had been satisfied. That seemed like a reasonable separation of responsibilities. The problem appeared when I examined how the evidence reached the verifier.

In one implementation path, the reasoning agent was responsible for deciding which operational information to retrieve. The deterministic verifier then evaluated the proposal against the information that had been collected. The decision itself was deterministic, but the evidence available to make that decision depended on the agent's earlier choices.

A test involving a simulated server, app-db-02, exposed the weakness. The governed Source of Truth reported RHEL 9.2, while the current observed state reported RHEL 9.4. The architecture contained a deterministic control intended to identify precisely that kind of conflict, but the agent retrieved only the Source-of-Truth record. The control accepted the scope because it never received the live facts needed to identify the disagreement.

The problem went beyond retrieval quality. It was architectural:

A deterministic decision is not necessarily a trustworthy decision if a probabilistic component controls whether the required evidence is available.

I revised the architecture to introduce what I called the Deterministic Acquisition Floor. Under this model, the deterministic side of the system becomes responsible for obtaining a minimum required set of evidence before consequential reasoning can proceed. Agents may still investigate additional information. They can retrieve context, explore relationships, and develop more informed recommendations. What they cannot do is determine whether the mandatory evidence required by a governing control will exist. This creates a clearer separation between discretionary investigation and required verification.

After introducing the floor, I repeated the conflict scenario. This time, the orchestrator acquired both records before the agent began reasoning, and the control correctly referred the disagreement for human review. Additional runs showed that a missing host produced an insufficient-evidence referral, while a clean, corroborated record could still proceed normally. The before-and-after evidence is published with the project's supporting research.

The broader lesson extends beyond infrastructure automation. Whenever an AI agent participates in a governed decision, we need to examine who makes the final decision and who controls the information required to make it correctly. A control that doesn't own its evidence dependencies may have less authority than its architecture suggests.

docs.title: A trusted enterprise system can contain untrusted information
docs.text:
The next finding developed from the other governing question: what information should the model be allowed to consume? The early context-integrity architecture distinguished between structured information from governed enterprise systems and unstructured natural-language content. Structured information could follow a trusted, typed path, while free-form content would pass through additional screening. This was a useful starting point, but implementation exposed a limitation: a governed enterprise system does not necessarily contain uniformly trustworthy information.

Consider a configuration management database. Its identifiers, lifecycle states, or controlled classification fields might be governed through established enterprise processes, and those fields can have meaningful authority within the systems that use them. The same record might also contain an operator-entered description, imported notes, or text populated by an external integration. Those fields do not automatically inherit the same semantic trust as the structured data around them.

The authority to write information into a system is not the same as establishing that the information is safe for an AI model to interpret as context.

This changed the context-integrity architecture. Rather than assigning trust primarily at the source level, Boundary moved toward classifying information at the field and content level. Governed typed fields could follow an appropriate structured path. Free-form natural-language content, even when retrieved from a governed source, required additional handling.

The Context Acquisition Gateway served as the governed entry point for information retrieved from enterprise systems and external sources. It constrained available acquisition mechanisms and preserved provenance. The architecture distinguished governed typed fields from free-form prose, with the latter requiring additional handling and screening where appropriate.

The gateway was implemented and exercised in selected prototype paths, including the deterministic acquisition floor. The intake path also distinguished structured operator declarations from model-inferred fields and recorded their provenance. These results establish specific acquisition and provenance behaviors. The published evidence does not independently establish comprehensive field-level classification across every gateway source and content type.

The semantic screener remained useful, but its role became more narrowly defined. It was one mechanism within a broader context-integrity architecture, not a general-purpose authority capable of declaring content safe.

The first real-model screening evaluation used four test inputs, or canaries, consisting of three deliberately constructed malicious examples and one clean control. These inputs had known expected outcomes, allowing me to examine how the screening model and its surrounding controls responded to suspicious and legitimate content.

Using Cisco's Foundation-Sec 1.1 8B security-focused language model, all three malicious examples were identified as suspicious through model judgment. However, the clean example produced no model verdict and was conservatively classified as suspicious by the deterministic fail-safe.

Subsequent implementation work exposed a different problem. An integration defect caused the web-intake screening path to evaluate a hardcoded test fixture rather than the operator-submitted input. That defect was corrected, and a deliberately suspicious input was used to verify the wiring. The earlier four-canary evaluation had exercised the model directly, before this later intake defect was encountered; its results did not depend on the faulty web path. A screener can produce a plausible verdict while evaluating the wrong information.

These findings reinforced why screening couldn't serve as an independent authority boundary. The model's judgment, the integrity of the path delivering its inputs, and the deterministic handling of its results all required separate consideration. They also shaped subsequent research into how information should be evaluated and admitted into an AI system's reasoning context.

docs.title: When failing safely leaves the operator stranded
docs.text:
Another architectural lesson appeared when the prototype began exercising stop conditions and recovery behavior. Boundary was designed to fail closed. If a required condition was not satisfied, evidence was missing, or appropriate authority could not be established, the system should not proceed with an infrastructure change. That principle remained sound. But working with the prototype exposed an operational problem: stopping safely did not always leave the operator with a useful next step. A workflow could correctly refuse to proceed while providing little help in understanding how the situation should be resolved. From the perspective of preventing unauthorized changes, the control was working. From the perspective of operating an enterprise system, it was incomplete.

This led to a more explicit treatment of the Advisory outcome. Advisory had been simply a label indicating that automation would not proceed. It became a legitimate operating outcome that needed to produce useful information for a human. When automated mutation was not authorized, the system could still provide a verified description of the proposed operation, the evidence available, the reasons automation could not continue, and the legitimate next actions. The human remained responsible for any subsequent operational decision. This preserved the security boundary while making the system more usable.

Recovery exposed a related issue. Once Boundary could change state within its simulated infrastructure environment, I needed to determine what should happen when a controlled operation failed or produced an uncertain result. The original authorization covered the planned action. It did not automatically authorize a second action simply because that action was described as rollback or recovery. Recovery may be intended to restore a system to a safer state, but it can still involve consequential infrastructure mutation, so it requires its own scope, evidence, identity, and authorization.

I revised the design so recovery could occur under a separate governed authority event. A human could authorize an eligible recovery strategy already bound to the verified operation, but could not invent an unrestricted new recovery action at the point of failure.

The prototype exercised several recovery conditions. In one case, recovery was refused because the system could not prove that the original operation had changed anything. In another, a separately authorized recovery operation completed. A third case exercised recovery failure, where the system stopped without submitting the later undo step. These were simulated-estate tests, not evidence of production recovery reliability, but they were sufficient to exercise the difference between a safe stop and an authorized recovery action.

The resulting principle was straightforward:

A safe stop prevents an unauthorized consequence. Governed recovery provides a controlled way forward without weakening that protection.

Enterprise AI systems need both.

docs.title: Autonomy is something the enterprise grants
docs.text:
One of the original goals of Boundary was to explore whether agents could eventually operate with greater autonomy as the system accumulated evidence of reliable behavior. It is tempting to think of autonomy as a property of the model. A more capable model might appear to deserve greater freedom to act, while a less capable model might require more human oversight. But model capability and operational authority are different properties. An enterprise might permit a particular class of routine, low-risk maintenance to proceed under standing authorization while requiring explicit approval for changes involving critical systems. That difference may have little to do with the model itself. It depends on the operation, its risk, its governing policy, and the evidence available to support a decision.

Boundary therefore modeled autonomy as a governed operating posture associated with bounded classes of work, and several concepts needed to remain separate. A workload tier established the maximum level of authority permitted for a class of operations. An autonomy lane represented the current operating posture. Transaction authorization allowed a human to approve a specific verified operation. Standing authorization represented a prior governed decision allowing a defined class of operations to proceed without a new approval for every qualifying transaction. The AI model could propose work within those arrangements, but could not independently assign itself a different tier, promote its authority, or create a new policy.

Implementation also demonstrated why one global autonomy setting was insufficient. An early design could apply a standing-policy envelope to a single class of work, but it was less effective when several workload classes needed to operate under different authority conditions simultaneously. I revised the architecture around a non-overlapping policy portfolio.

The resulting prototype exercised multiple authority outcomes through the same orchestrator. One workload could operate under valid standing authorization. Another could produce an Advisory outcome for human consideration. A third, lacking applicable authority, would refuse to execute. Each outcome followed its own governing conditions, which offered a more expressive model than treating automation as simply manual or automatic.

There was still a limitation. The architecture could represent different autonomy postures and enforce their authority boundaries, but it did not complete the full evidence-production and promotion lifecycle required for a workload to earn greater autonomy over time. That would require representative operational evidence, explicit promotion criteria, and accountable enterprise governance. The intended direction remained clear: autonomy should increase when evidence justifies a governed decision, and an agent's assertion that it is ready is no such evidence.

docs.title: What did the implementation actually demonstrate?
docs.text:
As Boundary developed, I tried to keep architectural ideas, implemented mechanisms, observed behavior, and unfinished capabilities clearly separate. This became particularly important because different parts of the architecture reached different levels of validation.

The semantic screening path was exercised using Foundation-Sec and the canary inputs described earlier. Those tests helped evaluate the bounded screening contract, but did not establish complete protection against prompt injection. The Deterministic Acquisition Floor was exercised in before-and-after prototype runs and published executable negative-path tests, including cases where required evidence was missing or conflicting. Transaction authorization, standing authorization, multi-lane operation, and Advisory behavior were exercised through the working prototype. The simulated estate also supported controlled execution and governed recovery.

Execution semantics required a separate investigation. Before defining the execution contract, I ran isolated probes of Ansible execution and rollback behavior to understand what its returned results actually represented. These were distinct from the integrated Boundary prototype, which used a simulated infrastructure estate to exercise orchestration, authorization, execution, and recovery.

One probe showed that a result could report that a change had occurred even though an attempted rollback failed before making the corresponding change to the host. Other probes exposed ambiguity involving reachability, transaction identity, and rollback behavior. Those observations reinforced why an orchestration system should not treat a tool's returned status as authoritative evidence of the actual infrastructure outcome without understanding its semantics. The execution contract was subsequently designed around those observed behaviors, but the production execution adapter was not built.

The last operator-accepted integrated prototype milestone was M6.3, the controlled-execution and governed-recovery checkpoint, which exercised those paths in the simulated estate. In this context, operator acceptance means that I personally conducted an integrated prototype acceptance walk, submitting operations and reviewing their behavior against the expected results. It does not imply acceptance by an independent operator or production organization.

The next checkpoint, M6.4, implemented and tested deterministic post-operation validation, but its operator acceptance walk was never completed. The remaining validation and learning stages were not built. The following table summarizes where the research stopped.

| Architectural area | Evidence status |

|---|---|

| Semantic screening | Exercised using Foundation-Sec and four canary inputs; full screening corpus not public |

| Context Acquisition Gateway | Selected acquisition and provenance paths exercised; complete field-classification coverage not publicly established |

| Deterministic Acquisition Floor | Integrated before-and-after runs and published executable negative-path tests |

| Transaction and standing authorization | Both authorization paths exercised within the integrated prototype |

| Multiple autonomy lanes and Advisory | Three policy outcomes demonstrated: standing authorization, Advisory, and refusal when no policy applied |

| Execution-result semantics | Investigated through real execution probes |

| Controlled execution and governed recovery | Simulated-estate acceptance walk; recovery-decision tests and 14 mutation probes reported in the M6.3 record |

| Deterministic post-operation validation | Implemented and tested, but not operator-accepted |

| Anomaly validation, final outcome recording, and learning | Not started |

| Production HA, policy lifecycle, evidence custody, and segregation of duties | Open architectural and engineering obligations |

Each kind of evidence supports a limited claim. A successful prototype execution establishes that a particular path was exercised under particular conditions. A mutation test can demonstrate that a control changes the outcome when removed or altered. An adversarial canary can show that a screening mechanism responds to a particular class of malicious input. None of those independently establishes production reliability, statistically meaningful detection rates, or operational safety across an enterprise environment. Boundary demonstrated several architectural mechanisms, but it did not establish a production-ready autonomous infrastructure platform.

docs.title: Why I stopped building
docs.text:
As the project developed, I periodically considered what additional implementation would contribute to the architectural investigation. Some additions were clearly worthwhile. Execution and recovery, for example, exposed questions that could not be answered adequately through diagrams or design discussions alone, and I needed to exercise those paths to understand the relationships among evidence, authorization, actual mutation, and recovery. Other work would have improved the completeness of the implementation without necessarily providing substantial new architectural insight.

By October 8, 2026, the remaining work was still meaningful engineering. Deterministic validation needed to complete operator acceptance. The later anomaly validation, final outcome recording, and learning stages had not been started. A real execution adapter, high availability, enterprise policy management, evidence custody, and segregation of duties would all require additional work before contemplating production use. These were legitimate requirements, but they increasingly represented the work of completing a product rather than testing the assumptions that had motivated the research. I had reached a point where further implementation was unlikely to materially change my understanding of the architectural boundaries, so I stopped.

This reflects how I approach independent architecture research. A research prototype does not need to become a finished product to accomplish its purpose. Sometimes the useful result is an implementation that demonstrates an architectural principle. Sometimes it is a test that exposes a flawed assumption. Sometimes it is the discovery that an apparently reasonable design does not enforce the boundary it claims to enforce. Boundary had produced all three kinds of evidence, and continuing to build simply because more functionality could be added would not necessarily have improved the research.

docs.title: The role of AI in the research itself
docs.text:
The research involved AI both as the subject of investigation and as a collaborator in developing the implementation. I used AI models and coding agents to help examine assumptions, develop alternatives, implement experiments, generate tests, and identify potential defects. That collaboration contributed to the project's progress, but it also raised a familiar question about accountability.

Identifying a potential architectural problem is different from deciding how the architecture should change. Generating an implementation does not establish that it conforms to the intended design, and a successful test result does not automatically validate the claim that motivated the test. Throughout the project, I attempted to keep those activities separate.

The surviving research record does not always establish precise authorship for every idea or intermediate decision, and I don't think it would be appropriate to reconstruct certainty where that evidence doesn't exist. What mattered was maintaining accountability for the architectural direction and using implementation evidence to evaluate whether the resulting system behaved as intended.

This closely mirrors the problem Boundary was investigating. In both cases, AI can contribute analysis, identify possibilities, and generate technically useful artifacts. The ability to contribute does not, by itself, establish the authority to make consequential decisions.

docs.title: What Boundary taught me about enterprise AI
docs.text:
The most useful results of Boundary were not specific to Linux patching. The patching scenario provided the operational context needed to investigate a broader architectural problem: how to introduce probabilistic reasoning into environments where authority, evidence, and operational consequences must remain accountable.

Capability and authority must remain separate, because a model's ability to recommend an action does not establish that the action is permitted. Source authority and content trust are also different properties, and a governed enterprise system may contain information that requires additional validation before entering an AI reasoning context.

Deterministic controls need dependable evidence. A control cannot reliably enforce its requirements if another component can decide whether the evidence needed to trigger it is acquired.

Boundary demonstrated how different workloads could operate under distinct, governed authority conditions. It also established an architectural direction for earned autonomy, where future promotion would depend on representative operational evidence and explicit enterprise authorization. That promotion lifecycle remains unvalidated.

Recovery was another tested authority boundary. The simulated-estate runs exercised refusal, separately authorized recovery, and recovery failure without permitting uncontrolled additional mutation. Those results support the narrower recovery-control claim, not a claim of production recoverability.

The conclusion that interests me most concerns the relationship between architecture and implementation. Drawing a diagram that shows AI reasoning separated from deterministic controls is easy. Establishing that the separation holds is considerably harder when information is incomplete, sources disagree, tools return ambiguous results, or an operation fails halfway through. Those conditions reveal dependencies and assumptions that are not always visible in a conceptual design. Boundary reinforced the value of implementing enough of an architecture to challenge its assumptions and to determine whether it actually expresses the properties we expect it to have, even if the result never becomes a finished application.

docs.title: Where the investigation leaves us
docs.text:
I expect organizations to keep exploring ways to give AI systems more responsibility for operational activities. Some of those applications will be low consequence. Others will involve infrastructure, security controls, financial operations, or systems where an incorrect action can have serious effects. As those use cases develop, I suspect the architectural conversation will need to extend beyond how capable individual AI models have become. We will need to consider what information those models consume, how their conclusions are verified, which authority boundaries govern their actions, and what happens when observations differ from expectations.

Boundary is no universal solution to those problems. It is a proposed architectural approach, supported by bounded prototype evidence, for separating reasoning from authority and keeping consequential actions subject to independently governed controls.

Looking back at the investigation, I keep returning to the two questions that came to define the work.

What do I trust the model to consume?

What do I trust the model's reasoning to influence?

For consequential enterprise AI, I think those are two of the most useful questions an architect can ask before deciding what to build.

docs.title: Project Bridging Human ↔ AI ↔ HumanExploring understanding, communication, and connection
docs.text:
Research status: Conceptual investigation — proposed framework and falsifiable research agenda. Not implemented or empirically validated.

Paper 1 — Conceptual framework: AI as a Scaffold for Human Connection: A Framework for Discovery and Communication (v0.4.2, 17 October 2026; not peer reviewed). Paper 2 — Research concept: Empowerment-Preserving AI Mediation (proposed empirical investigation; no study conducted).

docs.title: The question that started it
docs.text:
Some people enjoy sustained, exploratory conversations with AI and sometimes wish they could discover another human who would enjoy exploring the same questions. That does not make human–AI interaction an inferior experience or something to replace. Project Bridging explores whether AI might offer an additional, voluntary way to find mutually valued human conversations.

The question is not just whether two people have similar interests. They might approach unfamiliar ideas with compatible curiosity while disagreeing about the subject, or share an interest without enjoying the same style of discussion.

Can AI responsibly increase opportunities for meaningful human connection by identifying potentially compatible people and supporting their communication, without manufacturing compatibility, diminishing human agency, or creating harmful dependency on the intermediary?

A personal research perspective

docs.title: Why I'm Exploring This
docs.text:
My background is in technology architecture, where much of my work involves understanding complex systems, their interactions, and the boundaries that influence how they behave.

As I began exploring artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner, I became interested in something beyond its technical capabilities: whether AI might help us understand how people think, reason, and communicate differently.

That led to another question. What if AI could help people discover others with whom they share an unusual compatibility in curiosity, reasoning, or depth of conversation—people they might otherwise never encounter?

The possibilities extend beyond matching people. AI might also help people understand one another across differences in communication, language, and culture.

But there is a fundamental tension. The same AI that facilitates human understanding might also distort it, manufacture apparent compatibility, or foster harmful dependence that diminishes people's agency.

Project Bridging is my independent exploration of these possibilities and risks.

I don't know whether the central hypothesis is correct. That's what makes it worth investigating.

My interest is not in making people choose between human and AI interaction, but in understanding whether AI can help create human connections that might otherwise never happen.

docs.title: Proposed approach
docs.text:
With explicit and separate permissions, patterns from repeated human–AI conversations might contribute to provisional, contestable conversational representations. A discovery mechanism could use those patterns alongside stated interests and preferences to identify possible partners, explain a limited rationale, and offer only excerpts or summaries authorized for sharing. Both people would independently decide whether to communicate.

If they do, optional scaffolding might assist with translation or clarification, but it must not silently rewrite away real differences or make the AI's interpretation substitute for the participants' meaning. Some participants might always value ongoing assistance. Others may choose not to use it. Neither reduced AI use nor continued AI use is a goal in itself.

Proposed separation of Human Connection, Relational Assurance, and Governance and Data responsibilities. An unvalidated conceptual design, not an implemented safety system.

docs.title: What the working paper contributes
docs.text:
The paper separates existing evidence from proposed mechanisms, alternative explanations, and open research questions. It outlines falsifiable hypotheses for discovery, profile contestability, communication support, relational assurance, and participant-directed assistance. It asks whether the added information from longitudinal interactions improves real, mutually valued encounters beyond simpler interest, preference, and participant-choice approaches.

A single meaningful conversation could count as a positive outcome even if it does not become an ongoing relationship. Conversely, an impressive model-derived compatibility score is not evidence that two people actually connected.

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
No Project Bridging dataset, matching implementation, deployed introduction system, or effectiveness study is reported. Whether inferred conversational patterns generalize from AI conversations to human encounters, improve discovery, avoid privacy and interpersonal harms, or justify a three-plane architecture remains untested. A simpler system may prove better.

A separately scoped Paper 2 research concept, Empowerment-Preserving AI Mediation, proposes an empirical investigation of communication assistance and human agency. It is not a completed study or peer-reviewed empirical paper.

docs.title: Prompt Security Guardrails on a Single GPU
docs.text: Context: Independent AI infrastructure and safety research Status: Completed research series; conditional architecture decision Domain: AI guardrails, GPU co-residency, deterministic orchestration, prompt injection, inference resource constraints Repository: View the public research repository on GitHub

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
I tested whether a security-specialized language model could operate as a local prompt-risk guard for a co-resident reasoning model on a single 20 GB GPU.

The hardware constraint was deliberate. The investigation was not simply about whether two models could fit into VRAM. It examined whether both models could remain resident, whether guardrail latency was operationally tolerable, whether parallel inference improved throughput, and whether model-based safety decisions were reliable enough to control progression through the workflow.

The answer was conditional.

The models could remain co-resident with usable memory headroom, but inference needed to remain sequential. More importantly, the safety architecture became credible only after deterministic controls were placed around the model judgments.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Determine whether a constrained single-GPU platform could support:

  • a security-specialized guard model
  • a separate reasoning model
  • enough remaining VRAM for stable operation
  • acceptable sequential guardrail overhead
  • deterministic control over model-generated safety decisions
  • prompt-injection resistance strong enough to justify continued use

The goal was to evaluate the architecture as a system rather than treat successful model loading or individual guard verdicts as sufficient evidence.

docs.title: Architecture and Method
docs.text:
The tested workflow used three model stages:

  1. the guard model classified the incoming request
  2. the reasoning model generated a proposed plan
  3. the guard model reviewed that plan

Model outputs did not directly authorize progression.

Deterministic gates recomputed the guard's dispositions from structured evidence, and a deterministic plan scanner was added between plan generation and model review after testing exposed an injection path that the model-only review failed to stop.

Both models remained loaded on the same GPU, while the inference stages executed sequentially.

The research used scripted measurement and evidence capture for VRAM use, latency, throughput, guardrail scoring, contention behavior, and architecture validation.

docs.title: Co-residency was viable
docs.text:
The guard and reasoning models occupied approximately 16.6 GiB together on the tested 20 GB GPU, leaving roughly 3.9 GiB of measured headroom.

Repeated labs reproduced the model residency footprint closely enough to support co-residency as an architecture option on the tested platform.

docs.title: Parallel inference did not improve throughput
docs.text:
Running the two model processes concurrently did not produce useful GPU co-execution in the tested configuration.

Measured pipelining was slightly slower than sequential execution, indicating time-slicing rather than beneficial parallel inference.

Sequential execution therefore became an explicit architecture constraint rather than an assumed limitation.

docs.title: Model verdicts required deterministic enforcement
docs.text:
The initial guard contract produced dangerous effective false approvals in the evaluation battery.

Recomputing the model's structured verdict through deterministic orchestration reduced those effective false approvals from six to zero across the tested 19-case battery.

The result did not prove that the guard model was universally safe. It demonstrated that model judgment became more useful when authority remained outside the model.

docs.title: One successful injection exposed a missing control
docs.text:
A prompt-injection scenario passed the initial triage stage and was rationalized by the later model review.

That failure occurred at a point where no deterministic backstop existed.

A deterministic plan scanner was added at that boundary and subsequently caught both replayed injected plans in the validation run with sub-millisecond execution time.

docs.title: Architectural Finding
docs.text:
The central result was not that a security model could reliably act as an autonomous guard.

It could not.

The more defensible architecture treated the model as a noisy witness whose judgments informed deterministic controls.

Authority remained with the orchestrator.

This created a clearer separation between:

  • probabilistic model judgment
  • structured evidence
  • deterministic policy enforcement
  • human escalation
  • controlled progression toward execution

The GPU constraint also mattered operationally. Co-residency avoided repeated model loading, but sequential inference imposed a measurable latency cost and constrained the latency and throughput envelope of this particular single-GPU design.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
The research provides existence proofs rather than production safety rates.

The evaluation battery contained 19 hand-written cases in one domain, the successful injection represented a specific attack pattern, and the deterministic scanner detects a bounded class of patterns rather than semantic intent.

The parallel-inference result is also specific to the tested runtime and two-process configuration without NVIDIA MPS.

The measurements should therefore be treated as evidence about the tested architecture, not universal performance or security claims.

docs.title: What This Demonstrates
docs.text:
This project combined AI infrastructure constraints with AI safety architecture.

It began as a resource-placement question and evolved into a broader control-plane finding: successful model deployment is not enough when model output can influence infrastructure actions.

The resulting architecture separates judgment from authority and uses deterministic controls to validate, constrain, or reject model decisions before progression.

Those findings became a precursor to later work on governed agentic infrastructure and controlled AI-assisted operations.

The public repository contains all nine lab guides, evidence files, findings, architecture decisions, measurement and analysis scripts, reproduction guidance, and provenance describing how AI assistance was used during the research.
